[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.270] The Present Research

Given the need to gain a rounded understanding of interpersonal emotion regulation motives that is rooted in participants' everyday experiences as well as theory, we conducted a series of studies that integrate bottom-up and top-down elements. Study 2 used daily diary methodology to explore the frequency and co-occurrence of motives in different social interactions across 2 weeks.

Through these methods, the aim of this article is not to develop and validate a scale to measure regulation motives.

[PAPER_0034, relevance_score=0.262] Study 2: Motives in Everyday Life

Studies 1a and 1b documented a broad range of motives that participants reported for regulating their own and others' emotions. Study 2 aimed to explore the frequency and co-occurrence of these motives in everyday social interactions using daily diary method. This technique, wherein participants complete an end-of-day report about experiences they had during the day, is suitable for studying interpersonal emotion regulation for several reasons.

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.306] Motive Structure Exploratory Analysis

Following helpful comments in review, we conducted additional, un-pre-registered post hoc analyses to assess higher order clusters among the motives. Because some motives tended to co-occur more than others and appeared more conceptually similar, we were interested in exploring the structure of motives. To determine if the motives were distinct or if some motives could be combined to further streamline the taxonomy, we employed several methods. First, we used the Spearman-Brown prediction formula to estimate the internal consistency of each motive pair.

[PAPER_0040, relevance_score=0.417] Design and Procedure

The study consisted of a baseline survey on Day 1, followed by 14 consecutive days of daily diaries. All variables of interest were in the daily diaries.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.356] Daily Diaries

The daily diary portion began the day after participants completed the baseline survey. For 14 consecutive days, participants received a Qualtrics link to the day's diary between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m., which they had until 11:59 p.m. the same evening to complete. Each survey contained questions on participants' most significant social interaction of the day. If they did not have an interaction that day, they instead answered questions about a recent significant interaction, which were included for even branching.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.352] Minor disagreement between raters was resolved through discussion.

Quantitative analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.2.1) on 1,830 diaries (92% of diaries) in which participants reported having an interaction that day.4We calculated the frequency of motive items based on the number of observations in which they occurred and the number of participants who reported them at least once during the 14-day period.

To examine co-occurrence of motives at the person level, we first computed the person mean usage of each motive across the study for each participant.

[PREREG_0030, relevance_score=0.348] ATTENTION CHECKS We included attention checks in the baseline and 5 out of 14 daily diaries.

- Baseline. Participants who failed both instructional attention checks or an open-ended attention check would be excluded. The instructional attention checks were embedded in question matrices and required participants to respond with a specific answer on a Likert scale. Failing those attention checks involved responding with another scale item. The open-ended attention check asked participants to describe in one or two sentences the last social interaction they had.

[PREREG_0031, relevance_score=0.395] One coder would go over the responses and check for nonsense or irrelevant responses that do not answer the question. Any responses identified as nonsense or irrelevant would be checked and confirmed by a second coder.

- Daily diary. Participants who failed more than 80% of attention checks that they had completed would be excluded. For example, if participants completed all 5 surveys in which there was an attention check, and failed 4 of those 5 checks, they would be excluded from analysis. Each attention check required participants to respond 100 on a 0-100 slider scale.

The study consisted of a baseline survey on Day 1, followed by 14 consecutive days of daily diaries. All variables of interest were in the daily diaries.

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.269] Interpersonal Emotion Regulation Motive

If participants indicated no intention to regulate, they answered filler questions included for even branching. If participants reported an intention to regulate their own emotions through others, they were then asked: "Why did you turn to the other person(s) to change your emotions during this interaction? Participants could select one or more response options outlined in Table 3. Similarly, participants who indicated an intention to regulate someone else's emotions were asked, "Why did you try to change their emotions?" with response options outlined in Table 3.

[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.282] These response options were generated in Study 1a and refined in Study 1b. Their display was randomized for every survey. For both intrinsic and extrinsic regulation, participants could also indicate if they had another motive not listed and provide open-ended responses or if they had no motive.

Notably, in the present study, we presented affect-improving and affect-worsening motives together in one block for both intrinsic and extrinsic regulation.

Quantitative analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.2.1) on 1,830 diaries (92% of diaries) in which participants reported having an interaction that day.4We calculated the frequency of motive items based on the number of observations in which they occurred and the number of participants who reported them at least once during the 14-day period.

To examine co-occurrence of motives at the person level, we first computed the person mean usage of each motive across the study for each participant.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.271] Because the resulting means were not normally distributed, we calculated nonparametric correlations between all intrinsic motive items and all extrinsic motive items using Spearman's ρ.

To examine co-occurrence of motives at the occasion level, we calculated the ϕ coefficient for each motive pair using the R package psych (Revelle, 2022), as motive items were dichotomous variables. We could not compute within-person correlations, since many participants had zero variance across some variables. Within-person correlation calculation would thus result in a large amount of missing data.

[PAPER_0058, relevance_score=0.350] In addition to the preregistered descriptive statistics, we also explored the sources of variability in motives with intraclass correlation coefficient, following the method to calculate intraclass correlation coefficient for dichotomous variables by Raykov and Marcoulides (2015). Intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from .12 to .35, indicating that only 12%-35% of the variability in motive selection occurred between persons.

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.319] Motive Structure Exploratory Analysis

Following helpful comments in review, we conducted additional, un-pre-registered post hoc analyses to assess higher order clusters among the motives. Because some motives tended to co-occur more than others and appeared more conceptually similar, we were interested in exploring the structure of motives. To determine if the motives were distinct or if some motives could be combined to further streamline the taxonomy, we employed several methods. First, we used the Spearman-Brown prediction formula to estimate the internal consistency of each motive pair.

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.368] This formula estimates the reliability of a two-item scale and provide further information about whether any two motives appear to share the same latent construct (Eisinga et al., 2013). Second, we conducted nonmetric multidimensional scaling to two-dimensionally visualize patterns of dissimilarity between motives based on their presence or absence across regulation occasions (d'Angella & Hennig, 2022).
